meta.title: Who really said "My heart is, and always will be, yours"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edward Ferrars says it in the 1995 film. Emma Thompson wrote it — Austen refused to report the proposal at all.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'My heart is, and always will be, yours'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Austen. It is Emma Thompson’s line, scene 186 of her Oscar-winning screenplay.

answer.label: Not Jane Austen — actually Emma Thompson
answer.authorDates: born 15 April 1959 · English actress and screenwriter
answer.sourceLine: Edward Ferrars’s proposal in Ang Lee’s Sense and Sensibility (1995), written by Emma Thompson, who also plays Elinor. Her published screenplay ↗ gives the speech at scene 186 and ends it “that my heart is and always will be yours” — without the two commas the internet has since added. It is not in Austen, and it could not have been: in chapter 49 of the novel Austen pointedly declines to tell us what Edward said.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Edward Ferrars (Hugh Grant) — a fictional character

source.excerpt: EDWARD: Elinor! I met Lucy when I was very young. Had I had an active profession, I should never have felt such an idle, foolish inclination. At Norland my behaviour was very wrong. But I convinced myself you felt only friendship for me and it was my heart alone that I was risking. I have come with no expectations. Only to profess, now that I am at liberty to do so, that my heart is and always will be yours.
trail: Searched the Project Gutenberg text of Sense and Sensibility ↗ — and the other seven Austen texts — for “always will be”. Zero matches across the whole corpus.

Read Austen’s actual proposal scene, chapter 49. She refuses the speech outright: Edward’s errand “was only to ask Elinor to marry him”, and “how soon he had walked himself into the proper resolution… in what manner he expressed himself, and how he was received, need not be particularly told.” There is no novel line here to misquote — the film had to invent one.

Downloaded the full text of Emma Thompson, The Sense and Sensibility Screenplay & Diaries (Newmarket Press, 1995) ↗ and found the sentence at scene 186, quoted above. Thompson’s production diary, printed in the same volume, names it again: her entry for Friday 5 May records the line-up for “Hugh’s last scene (‘My heart is and always will be yours’)”.

Confirmed the credits against Wikipedia’s article on the film ↗: screenplay by Emma Thompson, directed by Ang Lee, produced by Columbia Pictures and Mirage Enterprises, US release 13 December 1995. Thompson won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for it.
source.cutTag: Scene 186 — INT. BARTON COTTAGE. PARLOUR. DAY.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the published screenplay. Note the punctuation: the script has no commas around “and always will be”. The comma-ed version everyone shares is a later tidy-up, which is a small sign that the line has been travelling by copy-paste rather than from the source.

source.rightsNote: In copyright, and the published book says so in as many words: its copyright page reads “Diaries copyright © 1995 by Emma Thompson” and “Screenplay and all other text copyright © 1995 by Columbia Pictures Industries, Inc.” — screen dialogue is work for hire, so the studio holds it, not the writer. Austen’s 1811 novel is public domain; this sentence is not in it, and is not covered by that.

author.bio: Emma Thompson (born 15 April 1959) is an English actress and screenwriter. Her adaptation of Sense and Sensibility won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay at the 68th Academy Awards, making her the only person to have won Oscars for both acting and screenwriting. She also plays Elinor Dashwood in the film.

copyAttribution: Jane Austen did not write “My heart is, and always will be, yours.” Emma Thompson did, for Edward Ferrars in the 1995 film of Sense and Sensibility (published screenplay, scene 186 — with no commas). In the novel, chapter 49, Austen declines to report the proposal at all. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Filed all over the internet under Sense and Sensibility, usually with a page reference nobody has checked. The novel has no such line, and a specific, documented person wrote it.

items.why: “always will be” returns no match anywhere in the novel ↗ or in the rest of Austen’s fiction.

She withholds the speech on purpose: “in what manner he expressed himself, and how he was received, need not be particularly told.” The famous line exists because Austen left a gap and a screenwriter filled it.
Scene 186 of her published screenplay ↗, and named again in her own production diary in the same book.

misattribution.truthLine: Right feeling, right characters, wrong century: the words are Emma Thompson’s, written for the 1995 film ↗ and Oscar-rewarded as an adaptation, not a transcription.

context.heading: The gap Austen left
lead: Austen almost never lets us hear a proposal. She reports that one happened, tells us how long it took, and moves on — the comedy is in the aftermath, not the declaration. Chapter 49 is the purest example: three hours pass, Edward secures his lady, and we are told his actual words “need not be particularly told”.

A film cannot do that. Somebody has to say something to camera. Thompson wrote the speech Austen withheld, and it has been circulating as Austen ever since — which is a backhanded compliment to how well she wrote it.
context.pull: The line exists because Austen refused to write it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Scene 186 of the published screenplay reads "that my heart is and always will be yours"; the diary entry for Friday 5 May names the line.
Sense and Sensibility ch. 49 says Edward’s manner of expressing himself "need not be particularly told"; "always will be" appears nowhere in the novel.
Emma Thompson wrote the screenplay, Ang Lee directed, Columbia Pictures produced, US release 13 December 1995, Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar.
Emma Thompson was born 15 April 1959 and is an English actress and screenwriter.
